title: How AI systems work
desc: Follow the input → model → output pipeline with hands-on examples
content_html:
What You'll Do

Every AI system, however clever it looks, is built from three parts: an input, a process in the middle, and an output. AI never works on its own — a person decides what goes in, what happens in the middle, and what comes out. In this project you'll learn to "see" those three parts inside the everyday AI tools around you, so AI stops feeling like magic and starts feeling like something you could design.

You'll Need

  • A whiteboard or a large sheet of paper
  • Sticky notes or index cards
  • A few everyday AI tools to think about (photo filter, voice assistant, video recommendations, map directions, spam filter)

Steps

  1. Draw the pipeline big: INPUT → AI SYSTEM → OUTPUT.
  2. Work one example out loud first. A homework reminder app: Input = your homework dates; Process = the app checks today against the calendar; Output = a reminder pops up.
  3. Pick three AI tools you actually use. On sticky notes, label the input, the process, and the output for each one.
  4. Check your work (swap with a friend if you can): does every example really have all three parts?
  5. Add a fourth box — Feedback — and work out how the output can loop back to become new input. When you tap "like," that choice becomes new data the recommendation system learns from.

Examples

AI toolInputProcessOutput
Photo filterYour selfieFinds your face, maps featuresEdited picture
Voice assistantYour spoken questionTurns sound to text, searchesA spoken answer
Video appWhat you watched beforeFinds similar videosYour "recommended" list

Tips

  • Keep it concrete — use real tools you actually use, not textbook examples.
  • Every time you catch yourself thinking "it just knows," stop and ask "what was the input, and who gave it?" That breaks the magic.
  • Remember a human designed each stage and chose the data. AI is a tool people build, not a mind of its own.

Think About It

  • For your favourite app, where does the input data come from — and did you choose to give it?
  • Who decides what a "good" output looks like?
  • What happens to the output if the input is wrong or missing?

Challenge Yourself

  • Easy: Map a video game you like as input → process → output.
  • Medium: Find an AI where the output becomes new input (a feedback loop) and draw the loop.
  • Hard: Sketch an AI you'd build to solve a problem at your school, labelling all three stages and the exact data it would need to learn from.
